en.g: a surname; probably of habitational origin, from the place named Bærum

1000691.etyen:
The place name continues Old Norse Bergeimr, a compound of berg (“rock, hill”) and heimr (“home, settlement, district”). Medieval records include the dative form Bergeimi in 1335; later historical spellings include Bergum. Rygh considers its use as a district name original or very old; a particular farm from which the district took its name has not been securely identified.
The components descend through Proto-Norse from Proto-Germanic *bergą (“rock, mountain”) and Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, settlement”), respectively. The first ultimately reflects Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“high; to r

en.g: a piece of flatbread spread with freshly churned butter

1004787.etyen:
From kinne (“to churn butter”) + kling (“flatbread or lefse spread with butter or sour cream”), literally “churned-butter flatbread”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kinnekling (“flatbread with freshly churned butter”).

en.g: goodbye, take care; a farewell expressing a wish for the addressee's well-being
x: Takk for besøket. Ha det godt!
morn, morn Bang, ha det godt, vi sees
bye, bye Bang, take care, see you

1005043.etyen:
A fixed phrase consisting of the imperative ha (“to have”), the pronoun det (“it”) and adverbial godt (“well”), literally “have it well”. As a farewell, the phrase expresses a wish for the addressee's continued well-being. The shortened farewell ha det (“goodbye, bye”) is an ellipsis of this expression or ha det bra (“goodbye, take care”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk ha det godt, Danish hav det godt and Swedish ha det gott (“goodbye, take care”).
